meta.title: When to Lay Sod in Michigan, Month by Month | HD Landscape
meta.description: Sod can go down in Michigan from mid-April through October if the ground is not frozen. Monthly timing, watering and the fall cutoff, from MSU Extension.

title: When to lay sod **in Michigan.**
lede: Sod can go down in Michigan from mid-April through the end of October, as long as the ground is not frozen. Spring and early fall are the easiest stretches. Late fall is the one to avoid. The ground matters as much as the date.
short: Michigan State University Extension says sod can be installed almost any time the ground is not frozen, from mid-April through the end of October.
Spring and early fall are the easiest stretches, because cooler weather means less watering.
Summer sod works, but it takes more water and longer to establish.
Late fall is the one to avoid. Roots need time to get into the soil before it freezes.
The soil should be moist and workable: not frozen, not soaked and not bone dry.

sections.h: Michigan's sod window runs mid-April through October
p: The window comes from Michigan State University Extension's sod bulletin, E-2911: almost any time the ground is not frozen, from mid-April through the end of October. Inside it, some stretches are a lot easier on the sod, and on whoever is holding the hose.

head: When
How it goes
Watch for
rows: January to mid-April
Too early. Wait for the ground.
Frozen soil, then soil too wet to work
Mid-April to May
A good stretch. Cool weather, less watering.
Wet clay. Wait until it crumbles.
June to mid-August
It works. More water, slower to establish.
Hot, dry, windy days dry sod out fast
Late August to September
A good stretch. Cooler nights, less watering.
Dry spells. Keep up with the water.
October
Still in the window, but the clock is running.
Earlier in the month is safer
November and December
Past the window MSU gives.
Roots need time before the soil freezes
table.note: Window from MSU Extension bulletin E-2911. Penn State Extension names spring, late summer and fall as the optimum times for sodding cool season grass.

after: Treat the months as a guide. Weather moves the edges a little every year, so go by the ground more than the calendar.

p: Late fall is the one time MSU warns against. Sod laid too late does not have time to root into the soil before it freezes, and sod that has not rooted is just sitting on the ground.

Penn State Extension says rooting can take up to 4 weeks, depending on the site and the weather. So a lawn laid in early October has some room. One laid in the last days of the month is cutting it close.
A fall lawn should be booked early. If the season runs out, the better plan is to wait for spring.

sections.h: Summer sod works, with more water
p: You can lay sod in a Michigan summer. Penn State Extension says sod can go down almost any time water is available, but midsummer heat means more frequent watering and a longer wait for it to establish. MSU says to be extra careful in hot, dry, windy weather, because new sod can dry out quickly.
So the real question for a July lawn is who is watering it. If you will be away, or you would rather not stand out there with a hose, we offer [plant watering](/plant-watering/) while it roots.

sections.h: What matters more than the date
p: A good date will not save bad ground. Four things decide how sod takes, and all of them come from the MSU bulletin.
list: **The soil can be worked.** Squeeze a small handful from about 4 inches down. If it cracks and starts to break apart when you relax your hand, it is dry enough to work.
**The soil is moist, not bone dry.** MSU says not to lay sod on very dry soil, because new roots get damaged moving into it. Moist is the goal. Saturated is not.

**The ground slopes away from the house.** MSU says a fall of 1 foot every 50 feet normally keeps water from standing on the lawn. If water sits in your yard, [yard grading](/yard-grading/) comes before sod.
**The sod goes down the day it arrives.** Sod builds up heat inside the rolls, and MSU says that can weaken the grass and even kill some of it. All of it should be laid on delivery day.
after: Clay is common across Metro Detroit, so that first test can hold a spring job back for a while after a wet stretch. A few days of waiting beats laying sod on mud.

sections.h: Water decides the first few weeks
p: The date only helps if the sod gets water. Penn State Extension calls lack of water the most common cause of sod deterioration. This is MSU's schedule in plain terms.

head: When
What to do
rows: First 30 minutes
Start watering.
First two weeks
Water at least once a day. Keep sod and soil moist, not soaked.
Hot, dry or windy days
Check it more often. New sod dries out fast.
Until it has rooted
Stay off it. Avoid heavy use until the roots are established.
Once roots reach the soil
Water less often, but more each time, to push roots deep.
Blades past 4 inches
First mow. Set the mower at 3 to 3.5 inches, with a sharp blade.
After 4 to 6 weeks of growth
Fertilize, following a soil test if you have one.
table.note: From MSU Extension bulletin E-2911, with Penn State Extension on keeping traffic off until the sod is well rooted. To check rooting, carefully lift the edge of a strip in a few spots.

after: We do not install sprinklers. If you have a system, use it. If you do not, MSU says hand watering usually lets you control the amount better than a mechanical sprinkler anyway. Jake calls after the job to talk through the watering, and our [watering guide](/journal/watering-new-plants-and-sod/) has the details.
On heavy clay, MSU also suggests core aeration 3 to 6 months after the sod goes in. We do not do aeration, so that one goes to a lawn care company.

sections.h: Sod has a longer season than seed
p: Seed runs on a tighter calendar. MSU's seeding bulletin, E-2910, puts the prime window at August 15 to September 15, with spring second and June 15 the last date. Sod has the whole stretch from mid-April through October, and MSU calls it the quickest and most reliable way to establish a lawn.

Shade is the one thing a good date will not fix. Most sod grown in Michigan is a Kentucky bluegrass blend, and the choice of grass on sod is limited. If shade is the problem, MSU suggests overseeding the established sod with a shade tolerant grass such as fine fescue. Some of those spots would do better as a bed, and Jake can say which.

sections.h: Count back from the day you want the lawn
p: A [sod job](/sod-installation/) starts with stripping the old grass, then grading, then laying. Many lawns are finished in a day, depending on the grade. After a wet stretch on clay, the real start date is the first day the ground can be worked.
To get on the calendar, call or text [(586) 718-8762](tel:+15867188762), or send a photo of the lawn. Jake will walk the yard and write up a free itemized estimate.
